To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca(2+) signaling is a stochastic process that can be described by a Markov chain and that the Ca(2+)-signaling system is a source of information.

Ca(2+) waves are generated by stochastic binding of ligands to the receptor and that Ca(2+)-induced Ca(2+) release is a stochastic process that is governed by a single parameter, the number of IP(3) receptors.
calcium oscillations originate by the stochastic binding to the receptors' binding sites and are spatially coordinated by wave nucleation, and that they are rich in information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new paradigm for calcium signaling, which is based on the stochastic properties of the elementary events and their spatio-temporal organization.
the question: how can we understand the stochastic dynamics of the Ca(2+)-oscillation system?
the stochastic properties of calcium oscillations and the determination of their internal properties from global observations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stochastic properties and the information content of calcium signals are determined by a few basic mechanisms.
the Ca(2+)-oscillatory signal contains a lot of information about the underlying processes and that this information can be used to extract parameters of the system.
the stochastic properties of the Ca(2+)-signalling system are determined by a few key parameters that are accessible from global observations of Ca(2+) signals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ca(2+)-oscillations are the consequence of a complex interplay between stochastic processes on the microscopic and macroscopic level.
the Ca(2+)-oscillations are a highly complex system with a rich internal dynamics and information content.
the information content of a Ca(2+) transient is not only determined by its amplitude, duration, frequency, or shape, but is also dependent on the stochastic nature of the Ca(2+)-signal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stochastic nature of Ca(2+) signals is a key element of the signal processing.
the information content of the Ca(2+)-oscillation pattern is much larger than the information content of single Ca(2+) transients.
Ca(2+) signaling is a stochastic phenomenon and that the cell is a complex system that can be described as an ensemble of interacting subsystems.
